To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the scattering cross section for liquid fat is 1.5 times higher than for water, and 1.2 times higher than for lean tissue.
the photon scattering cross-section data of freshly excised liquid pig fat, measured in the interval 0.02 < chi < 0.64A-1, can be exploited as an indicator of tissue composition.

(1) the photon scattering cross-section of fat is larger than that of muscle by a factor of 3 to 4 in the range of interest, (2) the photon scattering of fat is highly anisotropic in the forward direction, and (3) the photon scattering in muscle is highly isotropic in the forward direction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new noninvasive diagnostic technique for quantitatively assessing the lean/fat ratio and the fat content of tissue in vivo.
the development of an experimental technique for the noninvasive characterization of lean and fatty tissue in vivo.
developing a method for measuring the lean and fatty tissue compositions of human breast tissue.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that coherent scattering in lean and fatty tissues can be used to distinguish lean tissue from fatty tissue and that the scattering cross-sections of lean and fatty tissues are significantly different.
the photon scattering cross-sections for fat and water are different and that the differences are sufficiently large to be useful in vivo.

The main takeaway from our work is that
coherent scattering can be used to determine the amount of water and fat in lean and fatty tissue.
photon scattering is sensitive to the fat-water ratio in tissues and is therefore a promising tool for non-invasive tissue characterization.
